color-contrast.title: Text does not stand out enough from its background
color-contrast.explanation: Text with too little contrast is hard to read for people with low vision, in bright light or on a dim screen. Normal text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, large text at least 3:1.
color-contrast.fix: Darken the text or lighten the background (or the other way round) until the ratio reaches 4.5:1. For example, #767676 on white is the lightest grey that passes. Check the pair of colors with a contrast checker.

image-alt.title: Image has no text alternative
image-alt.explanation: A screen reader cannot describe an image that has no alt text, so people who cannot see it miss what it shows.
image-alt.fix: Add an alt attribute that says what the image shows or does, like alt="Bar chart of monthly sales". If the image is only decoration, use an empty alt="".

link-name.title: Link has no readable text
link-name.explanation: A link with no text or label is announced only as "link", so nobody can tell where it goes.
link-name.fix: Put readable text inside the link, or add an aria-label that says where it goes, like aria-label="Open the pricing page". Give icon-only links a label too.

button-name.title: Button has no accessible name
button-name.explanation: A button without a name is announced only as "button", so people who use a screen reader or voice control cannot tell what it does.
button-name.fix: Write visible text in the button. If it holds only an icon, add an aria-label, like <button aria-label="Close">.

label.title: Form field has no label
label.explanation: Without a label, people who use a screen reader do not know what to type, and the field is harder to click or tap.
label.fix: Connect a <label for="id"> to the field, or wrap the field in the label. Do not rely on a placeholder alone.

html-has-lang.title: Page does not declare its language
html-has-lang.explanation: Screen readers use the language of the page to choose the voice and the pronunciation. Without it, text can be read with the wrong accent.
html-has-lang.fix: Add the language to the root element, for example <html lang="en">.

document-title.title: Page has no title
document-title.explanation: The title is the first thing a screen reader announces, and the name shown in browser tabs and search results. Without it, people cannot tell pages apart.
document-title.fix: Add a short, unique <title> in the <head> that says what the page is about.

heading-order.title: Heading levels skip a step
heading-order.explanation: People who use a screen reader move through a page by its headings. A jump from h2 to h4 suggests that content is missing and breaks the outline.
heading-order.fix: Use the heading levels in order, one step at a time (h1, h2, h3). Choose the level for the structure, and set the size with CSS.

empty-heading.title: Heading is empty
empty-heading.explanation: A heading with no text is announced as an empty stop in the outline of the page, and confuses people who navigate by headings.
empty-heading.fix: Write the text of the heading, or remove the tag if it is only there for spacing. Use CSS for space.

page-has-heading-one.title: Page has no main heading
page-has-heading-one.explanation: An h1 tells people what the page is about, and gives screen reader users a place to jump to.
page-has-heading-one.fix: Add one <h1> with the main topic of the page, and use h2 and below for the sections.

landmark-one-main.title: Page has no main landmark
landmark-one-main.explanation: The main landmark lets people who use a screen reader or a keyboard skip the menus and go straight to the content.
landmark-one-main.fix: Wrap the central content of the page in one <main> element (or role="main").

region.title: Some content is outside any landmark
region.explanation: Content that sits outside a landmark is hard to find for screen reader users, who jump between landmarks like the header, the navigation, the main content and the footer.
region.fix: Put all the visible content inside landmarks: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <footer>, or sections that have a label.

select-name.title: Dropdown has no label
select-name.explanation: Without a label, people who use a screen reader do not know what they are choosing.
select-name.fix: Connect a <label for="id"> to the <select>, or add an aria-label.

input-button-name.title: Input button has no text
input-button-name.explanation: A button made with <input type="submit"> or similar needs a value, otherwise it is announced as a button with no name.
input-button-name.fix: Give it a value attribute, like <input type="submit" value="Send">.

input-image-alt.title: Image button has no text alternative
input-image-alt.explanation: An <input type="image"> works as a button, so a screen reader needs to be told what the button does.
input-image-alt.fix: Add an alt attribute that names the action, like alt="Search".

frame-title.title: Frame has no title
frame-title.explanation: Screen readers announce the title of an iframe, so people know what it holds before they go in.
frame-title.fix: Add a title to the <iframe> that describes its content, like title="Map of our office".

aria-hidden-focus.title: Hidden content can still receive focus
aria-hidden-focus.explanation: An element hidden with aria-hidden="true" that can still be reached is invisible to a screen reader but not to the keyboard, so the focus lands on something that is not read.
aria-hidden-focus.fix: Remove aria-hidden from the element, or make everything inside it unreachable (tabindex="-1", disabled, or hidden with display:none).

aria-roles.title: ARIA role does not exist
aria-roles.explanation: A role that is misspelled or invented is ignored, so assistive technology gets no information about what the element is.
aria-roles.fix: Use a valid ARIA role from the specification, or remove the role if a native element such as <button> already does the job.

aria-valid-attr-value.title: ARIA attribute has an invalid value
aria-valid-attr-value.explanation: An ARIA attribute with a value that does not fit, like aria-expanded="maybe" or an id that does not exist, is ignored or misleading.
aria-valid-attr-value.fix: Use a value that the attribute accepts (for example true or false), and check that the ids in aria-labelledby, aria-controls and similar attributes point to elements that exist.

aria-required-attr.title: ARIA role is missing a required attribute
aria-required-attr.explanation: Some roles need attributes to work: a checkbox needs aria-checked, a slider needs aria-valuenow. Without them, the state of the element is unknown.
aria-required-attr.fix: Add the attributes that the role requires, or use the native element (such as <input type="checkbox">), which handles them for you.

aria-allowed-attr.title: ARIA attribute is not allowed on this element
aria-allowed-attr.explanation: An ARIA attribute that does not belong to the role of the element is ignored or confuses assistive technology.
aria-allowed-attr.fix: Remove the attribute, or change the role or the element so that it is allowed. Check which attributes the role supports.

aria-input-field-name.title: Custom input has no accessible name
aria-input-field-name.explanation: A custom input, such as a combobox or a slider, with no name leaves people who use a screen reader guessing what to enter.
aria-input-field-name.fix: Add an aria-label, or point aria-labelledby to visible text that names it.

aria-command-name.title: Custom command has no accessible name
aria-command-name.explanation: An element with the role link, button or menuitem and no name is announced with its role only, without saying what it does.
aria-command-name.fix: Add visible text, an aria-label or an aria-labelledby that says what the command does.

aria-required-children.title: ARIA role is missing the child elements it needs
aria-required-children.explanation: Some roles are containers that must hold specific children, like a list that holds list items. Without them, the structure is broken for assistive technology.
aria-required-children.fix: Add the child roles that are required (for example role="listitem" inside role="list"), or use the native elements <ul> and <li>.

role-img-alt.title: Element with role img has no text alternative
role-img-alt.explanation: An element with role="img" is treated as an image, so it needs a text alternative.
role-img-alt.fix: Add an aria-label or an aria-labelledby that describes the image, or remove role="img" if it is only decoration.

svg-img-alt.title: SVG that works as an image has no text alternative
svg-img-alt.explanation: An SVG with role="img" is treated as an image, so a screen reader needs a text that says what it shows.
svg-img-alt.fix: Add a <title> inside the SVG or an aria-label, or aria-hidden="true" if it is only decoration.

list.title: List is not made of list items
list.explanation: Screen readers announce how many items a list has. A <ul> or <ol> that holds other elements makes that count wrong.
list.fix: Put only <li> elements (and script or template) directly inside <ul> and <ol>.

listitem.title: List item is outside a list
listitem.explanation: An <li> outside a <ul> or <ol> is not recognized as part of a list.
listitem.fix: Put every <li> directly inside a <ul> or an <ol>.

target-size.title: Tap or click target is too small
target-size.explanation: Small targets are hard to hit with a finger, a mouse or a tremor, and easy to press by mistake when they sit next to another one. WCAG 2.2 asks for at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels.
target-size.fix: Make the target at least 24x24 px with width, height or padding, or leave enough space around it. For touch, 44x44 px is more comfortable.

meta-viewport.title: Zoom is blocked on the page
meta-viewport.explanation: Blocking pinch zoom, with user-scalable=no or a maximum-scale below 2, stops people with low vision from enlarging the text.
meta-viewport.fix: Remove user-scalable=no and any maximum-scale below 2 from the viewport meta tag (a maximum-scale of 5 or more is better still): <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">.
